hook.text: Send every request to the cheapest model that passes.

passes.text: [curious] But passes what? Somebody has to write the test.

table.text: And every model launch comes with a table of scores that looks like one.

hook-in.text: So what are those benchmarks measuring?

families.text: Each is a fixed set of questions with known answers.

mmlu.text: MMLU is multiple choice across fifty-seven subjects, from elementary math to law.

gpqa.text: GPQA Diamond is graduate science: PhDs from other fields, even with the web, score about thirty-four percent.

swe.text: SWE-bench hands over a real GitHub issue, and the patch has to pass the project's own tests.

arc.text: And Arc AGI asks for the rule behind a few grid puzzles, or in version three, the rules of a game, by playing it.

read.text: Reading a score starts with where it sits on the scale.

mmlu-gap.text: On MMLU, ninety-two point three beats ninety-one point seven. But some of its answer keys are wrong, so about ninety-five is the most anyone can score.

noise.text: Six tenths of a point, that close to the ceiling, is noise.

arc-gap.text: On Arc AGI three, sixty-two point seven against thirty point two, with room above both, is a real difference.

read-in.text: That crowded ceiling is the first of four ways a launch table misleads.

saturation.text: One, saturation. Once everyone scores near the top, a test can't tell them apart.

sat-now.text: Every frontier model clears ninety-two on MMLU. GPQA Diamond, built to replace it, has its leaders around ninety-five.

sat-fast.text: And tests fill up fast. Humanity's Last Exam went from every model under ten percent to the best near sixty, in twenty months.

sat-tell.text: The tell: if every model in a row sits within three points, skip the row.

contam.text: Two, contamination. Test questions get published, published text gets crawled, and crawled text becomes training data.

memory.text: So a model that memorized the answers and one that can do the work report the same high score.

swe-drop.text: That's why OpenAI stopped reporting SWE-bench Verified in February: models could recite some of its fixes.

defense.text: The defense is a test it can't have seen: kept private, or newer than its training.

select.text: Three, selective reporting. A launch post picks its benchmarks, its rivals and its settings.

astra.text: Arc Prize ran GPT six Astra on Arc AGI three in two harnesses, the code wrapped around a model.

astra-scores.text: In Arc's standard one, sixty-two point seven. In OpenAI's, which kept its hidden reasoning between moves, ninety-nine point nine, for less money.

astra-same.text: Same model, same test, same week. Only the first number compares with anyone else's.

mismatch.text: Four, the deepest: construct mismatch. A benchmark measures performance on the benchmark, and that only carries over if your task looks like it.

transfer.text: Tasks like SWE-bench still predict agentic coding, because they look like the job. They say almost nothing about reading your invoices.

third.text: So a model that ranks third everywhere can still be the best one for you, and no leaderboard will say so.

checklist.text: Ask four things of any row. All within three points? Could the model have seen it? Whose harness ran it? Does the task look like yours?

own-in.text: If the last answer is no, there's one way to find out.

own.text: So measure it yourself. Collect real examples with known answers, run each candidate, score automatically, and compare.

howmany.text: [curious] How many examples? Fewer than you'd think.

sim.text: Take one model that's right eighty percent of the time and one that's right sixty-five. Score each on twenty examples, again and again.

twenty.text: The better one comes out ahead about four times in five.

fifty.text: With fifty examples, ninety-four times in a hundred.

close.text: And if two still look close after thirty examples, they probably are. Pick on cost.

harness.text: The harness is just a loop. Here are ten tickets, each with its right queue, and two stand-in models.

scores.text: The cheap one routes three of them right. Thirty percent. The other gets all ten.

misses.text: But read the misses. The cheap one sent all seven to other. Whether that hurts depends on who reads that queue.

freetext.text: Free text is harder to score. First choice: make the output checkable, with fields to compare.

props.text: Next: score properties. Say it writes a summary: does it name the three facts, and stay under the limit?

judge.text: Last: have a strong model grade it on a rubric, knowing judges favor longer answers.

cost.text: Then put cost beside accuracy. Say four tiers score ninety-one to ninety-five percent on a million requests a month.

cost-gaps.text: Opus buys one point over Sonnet, for twice the money. Fable buys nothing over Opus, at two and a half times the price.

cost-error.text: So price the errors. Sonnet's three points mean thirty thousand fewer a month, at about five cents each.

end.text: Build that harness once, and it outlives every model in it.

last.text: When the next one launches, skip its table. Run your examples, and in an hour you'll know if it's good enough.

cost-verdict.text: If a mistake costs even a minute of someone's time, the cheap model is the expensive one.
